info.bio: Lou Reed (nacido como Lewis Allen Reed el 2 de marzo de 1942 en Freeport, Long Island, Nueva York - 27 de octubre de 2013) fue un cantante y escritor de rock, considerado el padre del rock independiente, primero como líder del grupo The Velvet Underground y luego en solitario. Enormemente influyente en el arte pop desde la década de los 60, sus principales discos son Rock'n Roll Animal, Transformer y, para un primer acercamiento, el soberbio concierto que ofreció en el Meltdown Festival: Perfect Night Live in London.

scenes.name: 1966: el año del single
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El libro son doce ensayos, uno por mes, cada uno a partir de un single. 1966 fue el último año en que el 45 fue la forma principal del pop, antes de que Sgt. Pepper’s convirtiera el LP en la fuerza creativa y comercial en el verano de 1967: en dos o tres minutos cabían ideas, actitudes, letras y experimentos que después se estirarían en álbumes de cuarenta minutos. El pop dejó de ser comercio, romance adolescente o diversión para volverse una experiencia total, «la única cosa viva» según Lou Reed, y el prisma con el que se interpretaba el mundo. El año empezó en el pop y acabó en el rock; empezó en la Gran Sociedad de Johnson y acabó con el resurgir republicano. Hubo ambición, aceleración y compresión, y una reacción proporcional de quienes veían que todo cambiaba demasiado deprisa. Savage, que cumplió trece años ese verano escuchando Radio Caroline South, se ciñe a los singles, sobre todo los que entraron en las listas de Billboard y Record Retailer, y deja fuera el free jazz, el minimalismo, el ska, los happenings y los situacionistas.

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Lou Reed quería llevar al pop la mirada sin concesiones de Burroughs, Purdy y Selby (heroína, prostitución masculina, vida gay y travesti) y amaba el doo-wop, el R&B profundo y el «Sally Go Round the Roses» de las Jaynetts: para él la música era «la única cosa viva». John Cale venía del Dream Syndicate de La Monte Young, con sus drones meditativos; Reed ya había grabado una obra maestra del dron de una nota, «The Ostrich». Tocaban delante de películas en la Cinematheque de Jonas Mekas cuando Warhol los adoptó a finales de 1965 y Paul Morrissey les impuso como cantante a Nico, la «Pop Girl» de 1966. Su carta de presentación fue tocar ante 350 psiquiatras («un tratamiento de electroshock»); después vinieron Uptight y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable en el Dom de St Mark’s Place (abril): luces, estroboscopios, Screen Tests, bola de espejos, la danza sadomaso de Malanga y Woronov y drones a un volumen insoportable. En California chocaron con la escena local («ellos iban de ácido, nosotros de anfetamina»; Gleason los llamó camp y enfermos). Su primer single en Verve, de Tom Wilson, «All Tomorrow’s Parties» / «I’ll Be Your Mirror» (julio), un producto pop art total, no tuvo ni reseñas ni radio. Eran un espejo de la América de 1966 que casi nadie quiso mirar.

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y sus herederos
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: La línea de art rock que reivindica el postpunk no es la del progresivo sinfónico sino la que va de The Velvet Underground al krautrock y al glam intelectual, fiel al principio minimalista «menos es más». Durante el «páramo» de los setenta, un racimo de espíritus afines unidos por su deuda con la Velvet (Lou Reed, John Cale, Nico, Iggy Pop, Bowie, Eno) colaboró en distintas combinaciones y sostuvo a los hipsters.
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

scenes.name: Metal industrial y post-industrial
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Uno de los logros clave de finales de los ochenta: la fusión de música industrial con hard rock y heavy metal, iniciada por los suizos Young Gods (samples de guitarras metálicas) y KMFDM. Chicago la completa: Ministry de Al Jourgensen (The Land Of Rape And Honey, «Jesus Built My Hot Rod»), Revolting Cocks, Pigface de Martin Atkins y, de ahí, Nine Inch Nails de Trent Reznor, que cambia el destino del industrial (Pretty Hate Machine, The Downward Spiral). El post-industrial: Neurosis, Steel Pole Bath Tub, Cop Shoot Cop, Missing Foundation, Pain Teens, Godflesh de Justin Broadrick, y los proyectos de Jello Biafra (Lard, Tumor Circus).

scenes.name: Space-rock y psicodelia extrema de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fundiendo los estilos psicodélicos que preferían la jam libre (acid-rock, space-rock, raga-rock), muchos grupos esculpen empresas sonoras épicas: Fuzzhead, Crawlspace, Pressurehed, Farflung, Fuxa, Gravitar (el Metal Machine Music de Lou Reed con ritmo), Pelt, Primordial Undermind, Escapade y, por encima de todos, Bardo Pond (Bufo Alvarius, Amanita) y Hash Jar Tempo. Texas recupera la supremacía de la locura psicodélica (Ed Hall, Cherubs, ST 37, Mike Gunn, Charalambides, Linus Pauling Quartet, la Vas Deferens Organization de Dallas); San Francisco, la psicodelia ruidosa de Mason Jones (Trance, Subarachnoid Space). En Nueva Zelanda, Roy Montgomery (Dadamah, Dissolve), Dean Roberts, Flies Inside The Sun; en Japón, Kousokuya, Mainliner, Musica Transonic, Acid Mothers Temple, Ghost.

scenes.name: La segunda venida del industrial
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los noventa el estilo brutal de Nine Inch Nails lo invade todo en EE UU y el industrial se vuelve fenómeno de masas; el «aggro» de KMFDM es menos visible pero igual de ubicuo: Grotus, Filter, Stabbing Westward, Acumen, Skrew, Electric Hellfire Club, Society Burning, Gravity Kills y, lo más original, Girls Vs Boys (Venus Luxure No.1 Baby) y New Wet Kojak. La EBM internacional se vuelve más brutal (Leaether Strip, Suicide Commando, :Wumpscut:, Hocico, Mentallo & The Fixer). La «música de la fábrica de la muerte» sobrevive en los escultores de ruido: los neozelandeses Dead C (Harsh '70s Reality, «música imposible de escuchar»), Gate, Bruce Russell, Namanax, Illusion Of Safety, Maeror Tri, Towering Inferno (Kaddish). Y el «digital hardcore» de Atari Teenage Riot y Alec Empire.

scenes.name: Doom, super-doom y stoner rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El doom (exageración lenta, gótica y barroca de los grooves de Black Sabbath) crece en Inglaterra: Paradise Lost, Cathedral (las largas suites líricas de Forest Of Equilibrium), My Dying Bride y Electric Wizard, que infla la pesadez hasta que la música ya no fluye, solo retumba (Come My Fanatics, Dopethrone); Orange Goblin, Katatonia. El «super-doom» de los Melvins sigue en Seattle con Earth (drones colosales entre La Monte Young y monstruos extraterrestres), Karp, Sunn, y el «sludgecore» del Sur (Eyehategod, Harvey Milk). El stoner rock: Kyuss, Queens Of The Stone Age, Sleep, Fu Manchu, Monster Magnet, Wellwater Conspiracy, Boris.

podcast.title: Staff Songwriter at Pickwick Records (September 1964)
podcast.body: In September 1964, Reed returned to Manhattan and secured a job as a staff songwriter at Pickwick Records. He was paid $25 a week to produce songs for budget albums, which were sold for a dollar in department and furniture stores. "By September 1964, he was back in Manhattan where he got a job as a staff songwriter at a label called Pickwick Records."

podcast.title: Bum-Biting Incident – Buffalo Concert, March 24, 1973
podcast.body: While performing a concert in Buffalo, New York, on March 24, 1973, a fan jumped out of the audience mid-set, screamed "leather," and bit Lou Reed on the buttocks. Security grabbed the fan and ejected him from the venue. Lou was forced to continue performing the rest of the show with a noticeably tender rear end. The incident reflected the kind of extreme, unpredictable audience behavior Reed attracted in New York underground circles. "Lou had to play the rest of the show with a rather tender button."

podcast.title: Electroshock Therapy in Youth (Late 1950s)
podcast.body: As a freshman at New York University, Lou Reed's parents were deeply alarmed by what they perceived as his antisocial tendencies. Some stories suggest their concern was specifically that Lou was "tipping towards homosexuality," leading them to send him for electroshock therapy in the late 1950s. This treatment was based on a contemporary theory that homosexuality could be "cured" by jolting the brain with electricity. This traumatic experience caused Reed to resent his parents for the rest of his life. "there was a theory that homosexuality could be cured with the right treatment, which in this case involved attaching electrodes to your head and jolting your brain with electricity."

xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Careers
xref.body: After the band scattered, Lou Reed pursued a successful solo career, John Cale made his own records and produced for others, Sterling Morrison worked as a tugboat captain before earning a PhD in medieval literature and working at a university in Texas, and Mo Tucker released solo records before working as a greeter at Walmart in Douglas, Georgia, to support her five children. "Everyone scattered. Lou had his successful solo career. John Kale made his own records and produced albums for others."

xref.title: Real Name and Nickname Origin
xref.body: Sid Vicious's birth name was John Simon Richie. His friend Johnny Lydon (Johnny Rotten) gave him the nickname "Sid" after Lydon's pet hamster. The "Vicious" part of his name was inspired by a Lou Reed song. Despite being initially "quite a gentle guy," Richie felt compelled to live up to the "Vicious" title.

xref.title: School Dislike and Early Drug Use
xref.body: Despite his intellectual interests, Ian hated school, preferring to stay home with his books and records by Iggy Pop, The Doors, David Bowie, and Lou Reed rather than attend class. Obligatory visits to local retirement homes with classmates were depressing but also led to rifling through medicine cabinets for medication. "Ian hated school. xref.title: Sterling Morrison's Academic Pursuits and Diverse Careers
xref.body: Sterling Morrison began his academic journey as an English major at Syracuse University, where he met Lou Reed. Though he did not graduate at that time, he completed his studies at City College in New York City in 1970. Following the official end of The Velvet Underground a year later, he enrolled at the University of Texas at Austin, where he earned a PhD in medieval studies. He then secured a teaching position in Texas until the mid-1980s. "Sterling was an English major at Syracuse University, which is where he met Lou Reed."

xref.title: World's First True Alternative Band (Late 1960s-Early 1970s)
xref.body: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, The Velvet Underground, led by Lou Reed, was recognized as potentially the world's first true alternative band. Their music was characterized by kinky themes, delving into topics of "weird sex and drugs and rock and roll." "Through the late 60s and early 70s, Lou was the leader of the Velvet Underground, which might have been the world's first true alternative band."

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."
